utterance: Hi Mark, I'm the doctor. I can see you've been dealing with a cough and fever for a few days — let's get to the bottom of it. First, tell me in your own words what's been going on: when did it start, and how have you been feeling?
reply: It has been going on for three days now. It was a dry, hacking cough to start with, and I have been burning up on and off, roasting even though I did not have a thermometer. Since yesterday I am bringing stuff up that is a rusty, brownish colour, though it was clear at first. I also got a sharp pain low down on the right side round towards my back yesterday, and it catches me when I take a deep breath or cough.

utterance:
Here's the plan, Mark. You have pneumonia — an infection in the lower part of your right lung. That explains the fever, the rusty-coloured phlegm, and the sharp pain when you breathe in, which comes from the inflamed lung lining rubbing. The good news is you're young and otherwise healthy, your blood pressure is fine, you're thinking clearly, and your oxygen level is acceptable — so you're safe to be treated at home rather than in hospital.

I've prescribed two things: an antibiotic called amoxicillin — two capsules three times a day for five days, and it's important you finish the whole course even if you feel better after a couple of days; and paracetamol — two tablets up to four times a day for the fever and the chest pain. Rest at home, keep your fluids up, and stay off work for at least a few days — I'm happy to give you a medical certificate.

With treatment, your fever should settle over the next two to three days, but the cough and tiredness can hang around for two to three weeks — that's normal and doesn't mean the antibiotics aren't working.
reply: Two to three weeks? I have exams coming up, so I really need to be back at school before then.

utterance:
I understand — and it likely won't be that long before you're back. The cough can linger for a few weeks, but most people are well enough to return to work within about five to seven days, once the fever has settled and their energy is coming back. Going back with a bit of a lingering cough is fine as long as you feel up to it. I'll give you a certificate for the rest of this week, and we can extend it if needed.

Now, the important safety net: please come back straight away — or go to the emergency department after hours — if you get more short of breath, if you cough up blood, if you become confused or very drowsy, if you can't keep fluids down, or if you're feeling worse overall rather than better. And if you're not clearly improving within 48 hours of starting the antibiotic, I want to see you again — your wife can drive you in. I'd like to check in with you in two days anyway, either by phone or in person, to make sure you're on the mend.

One last thing: once you're fully recovered, I'd recommend getting your flu vaccine — it's not too late in the season, and this illness shows how miserable a respiratory infection can be. Do you have any questions about any of that?
reply: That sounds fair enough, I will just take the certificate and follow the instructions.

utterance: All right, Mark — here's your script for the amoxicillin and paracetamol, plus your medical certificate. Start the antibiotic as soon as you get it, rest up, and keep the fluids coming. I'll see or speak with you in two days, and remember: worse breathlessness, coughing blood, confusion, or not improving in 48 hours means you come straight back or head to emergency. Take care, and I hope you feel better soon.
